stories.title: Iran seized cargo ship over Hormuz pollution
stories.summary: Iran seized a bulk carrier for dumping oil, burnt oil, bilge water, and industrial sludge into the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian authorities. The polluted waste has been cleaned, and the ship has been referred to the judiciary, with Iran demanding compensation for recent oil spills. Iran plans to charge fees from vessels transiting the Strait to fund services like environmental protection, despite strong US opposition to these fees. Iranian authorities have seized a bulk carrier after they said it dumped oil and sludge into the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported on Aug 31. “Following the publication of images of the discharge of oil into the sea... expert and clean-up teams were dispatched to the site and seized the ship causing the pollution,” the deputy head of the Ports and Maritime Department of the southern Hormozgan province, Esmaeil Makizadeh, told the official IRNA news agency. “The seized ship was a bulk carrier carrying sugar and had dumped a mixture of burnt oil, bilge water and industrial sludge directly into the sea,” he added, without specifying the vessel’s flag or the nationalities of its crew. He said the waste has since been cleaned from the water and the ship has been referred to the judiciary. Iran has demanded compensation following several oil spills in recent weeks, including near the country’s Qeshm island. Early in August, an oil slick was also spotted near neighbouring Oman from a tanker that ran aground. An AFP investigation found the ship had been stranded for weeks near Oman’s Al-Qibliyyah island after it was damaged by explosions. Iran has maintained control over the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the Middle East war in February.

stories.title: Why EU-Israel data-sharing deal must be quashed
stories.summary: Why EU-Israel data-sharing deal must be quashed Submitted by Raja Natour on Fri, 08/28/2026 - 17:08 By enabling the exchange of sensitive personal information, the draft agreement would heighten the dangers facing Palestinians Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu shakes hands with a top EU official during a news conference in Brussels on 11 December 2017 (Emmanuel Dunand/AFP) On I recently found myself wishing that every official who pushed for a data-sharing deal between Europol and Israeli police would have to walk through the world knowing that every intelligence agency in Europe - and beyond - had access to the most intimate details of their private lives; that they, too, would live
article_sentences: I recently found myself wishing that every official who pushed for a data-sharing deal between Europol and Israeli police would have to walk through the world knowing that every intelligence agency in Europe - and beyond - had access to the most intimate details of their private lives; that they, too, would live with the constant fear that this information could be used against them at any moment, anywhere.

This is exactly the reality that the European Union is preparing for millions of Palestinians: to turn their lives into open books for Israeli authorities, forcing them to navigate the world under perpetual threat and surveillance.

In 2022, it appeared that negotiations between the EU and Israel over an operational police cooperation agreement had reached an impasse, largely due to questions over its application to the occupied territories - namely the West Bank, the Golan Heights and the Gaza Strip.

Yet despite the fact that the draft agreement contains a highly problematic and dangerous clause in which the EU would share sensitive personal information about Palestinians with Israel, a new investigation has revealed that talks continued at least until this past January - despite the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
Europol has long assisted EU member states with information sharing, intelligence analysis, and security coordination involving Israel.
In 2005, the EU council designated Israel as a “priority partner” - a puzzling move, given Israel’s status as an occupying power that routinely violates international law.
Europol subsequently began formal negotiations for a cooperation agreement with Israel.
But the talks were reportedly stalled by concerns over Israel’s compliance with EU data protection standards and the location of Israel’s police headquarters in occupied East Jerusalem.
I must admit, when I read that these were among the EU’s key concerns, I wondered how such questions could still be up for debate.
The EU and Europol know perfectly well that Israel does not comply with international treaties and law.
Why is the question not whether Israel should have access to sensitive personal data about Palestinians in the first place?
Why should Palestinians have to live with the knowledge that any police officer or Shin Bet agent could know their sexual orientation or intimate personal details?

stories.title: Bloomberg records biggest monthly rise in agricultural commodity prices since 2012
stories.summary: Wheat was one of the main drivers of the increase, with prices recently reaching a three-year high
article_sentences: NEW YORK, August 31.
Conflicts and weather conditions pushed agricultural commodity prices to their biggest monthly increase in August in 14 years.
According to the Bloomberg Agriculture Spot Index, which tracks 10 major agricultural and food commodities, the index added 13% last month and reached $434.
Wheat was one of the main drivers of the increase, with prices recently reaching a three-year high due to the situation involving Black Sea ports, the report said.
In late August, the price of a bushel of wheat (27.2 kg) rose to $7.79, the highest level since February 2023.

According to a report by analytics and consulting company Lachstock Consulting, if exports from the Black Sea basin do not resume, the market will increasingly face the problem of supplies across multiple seasons rather than a short-term logistics issue.
Another problem Bloomberg cited is poor weather caused by climate change: summer heat damaged corn crops in the US and Europe.
Additional risks to next year's crops, including cocoa beans, will be posed by the El Nino climate phenomenon, which affects global weather.
